channel.title: Africa Global Forum — Reports
channel.description: Free research from Africa Global Forum on the Africa ⇄ Abroad corridor — remittance, migration, capital, entrepreneurship, culture and industrialisation.

item.title: Twenty Countries Listen. Four of Them Pay.
item.description: Where is African music actually listened to outside Africa? One song is certified in twenty-two countries — 5m units in the US, 1.8m in the UK, 1.56m in India, Diamond in Poland — and has been number one in eight, from the Netherlands to Romania. Set against where the money is, which African nationalities are actually abroad, and where the live circuit runs. Eleven charts and a four-tier scorecard.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Music Is African. The Money Is Abroad.
item.description: Spotify pays about $300 for a million streams in Nigeria and $10,000 for a million in Sweden — a 33× gap on the same song, the same day. One platform paid Nigerian artists $44.3m in 2025, more than the entire tracked Nigerian market is worth. Why the diaspora is not Afrobeats’ audience but its business model.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: How Long Until It Was Worth It? — How Hard It Really Is for Africans to Succeed Abroad (2026)
item.description: Workers of sub-Saharan African origin face a 26.1% pay gap — against 9.0% for European arrivals in the same countries. Three-quarters of it is not getting the same jobs, not being paid less for them. Four rungs, a year-by-year timeline, top destinations, and eleven countries scored — including Australia, Asia and the Gulf, where the ladder ends at rung two.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Who the Diaspora Actually Marries — Intermarriage Among Africans Who Moved Abroad to Study or Work (2026)
item.description: African immigrants are among the most educated migrant groups on earth and among the least likely to marry outside their group — which breaks the standard model entirely. The gender gap, the generation ladder, and why arriving to study differs from arriving for work.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: More Africans Move to Africa Than Leave It — The Diaspora, Counted (2026)
item.description: 20.7 million Africans live outside the continent — and 25 million moved to another African country. Where they are, how many are working and studying, why they went, and the question nobody asks: between 20% and 50% of all immigrants leave within five years.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Your Address Pays Better Than Your Following — Which Social Platforms Actually Earn Africans Abroad Money (2026)
item.description: TikTok’s payout programme runs in about ten countries and none are African — so the diaspora gets paid where home cannot. The real rates on YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and X, what $1,000 a month actually takes on each, and why 112 paying supporters beat 100,000 views.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Where the Door Is Actually Open — The Countries With the Best Policy for Africans Moving Abroad (2026)
item.description: Germany charges €0 tuition and lets you arrive without a job. Ireland gives family rights on day one at a €36,848 graduate salary. Portugal has a route most Lusophone Africans have never used. A policy-by-policy read of where Africans can actually study, work, bring family and settle.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Visa Treadmill — What It Costs to Stay Legal (2026)
item.description: £77,414 in Home Office fees for a family of four on the UK’s 10-year route — arriving as six sudden five-figure demands, not a monthly bill. Every figure from published government schedules, plus the same build for 25 other countries across Europe, North America, Asia and Africa.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Africa Saves. It Just Doesn't Compound. — Household Saving and Investment in Africa's 10 Largest Economies (2026)
item.description: Egypt saves 1.2% of GDP. South Africa’s households save less than nothing. Yet 17 million savings groups serve 200 million members. How households save across the ten largest economies, why the gap persists, which countries broke the pattern — and a practical playbook for the diaspora.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Faith in the Diaspora — Why Africans Abroad Lose (or Transform) Religion, and What Replaces the Church (2026)
item.description: Participation goes first, personal importance second, affiliation last. Why Africans abroad lose — or transform — their sense of religion, and the portfolio of chamas, WhatsApp groups, gyms and networks replacing the church. Merged, expanded & fact-checked edition.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Banks That Let Africans in the Diaspora Invest From Where They Live (2026)
item.description: $95–100bn flows home every year, mostly spent, not invested. 12 diaspora banking programmes, 3 government bonds and 4 licensed apps — scored on remote onboarding, real investment products, and what customers actually say about trust.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Setting Up a Remittance Fintech in Europe — A Market-Entry Guide for African Founders (2026)
item.description: Nothing in EU or UK law stops an African founder from owning a licensed payments company. Everything else is the hard part — ranked across 10 markets, with LemFi, Flutterwave and Moniepoint as case studies.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Sense of Time — Africa and the Western World (2026)
item.description: “When everyone has arrived” vs “14:00, sharp.” Two coherent philosophies of time — the event and the clock — where each came from, how they collided under colonialism, how each prices a day’s work, and how the diaspora runs both.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Marrying Across Borders — The 20-Year Rise of the Price of Being Together (2026)
item.description: In 2006: no income requirement, fees of a few hundred pounds. In 2026: a £29,000 bar half of UK workers can’t clear, quadrupled fees, and four-year US waits. Twenty years back, twenty years forward — and the playbook.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Other Side of the Bet — How Hard Is the Job Hunt in the Countries Africans Study In? (2026)
item.description: Canada’s youth unemployment: 14.7%. US recent grads: doing worse than the workforce. UK: 140 applications per graduate job. How hard the job hunt is where Africans study — for the locals themselves — and the playbook for beating it.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Degrees of Debt — What Africans Pay to Study Abroad, and the Job That Has to Pay It Back (2026)
item.description: 500,000+ Africans study abroad — at up to $60k a year, on 13%-interest loans that run up to 20 years. The whole bet rests on turning the degree into a job. What it costs, when it pays, and when it traps.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Wealth We Leave Behind — African Diaspora Money That Never Comes Home (2026)
item.description: The diaspora saves ~$53bn abroad every year — and the systems for bringing it home barely exist. Lost pensions, frozen pensions, zero US–Africa agreements, and the one-evening checklist that protects your family.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Support Money vs Ownership Money — Where Africa's $100bn in Remittances Goes (2026)
item.description: Africa received a record ~$100bn from its diaspora in 2024 — and ~72 cents of every dollar is consumed the year it lands. What the gap costs, and the ~$125bn prize for shifting just 12 cents of it.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Living Room vs The Bedroom — How Africa's Top 10 Economies Allocate Household Spending (2026)
item.description: Money spent on what others see vs money spent on what builds you. Across nine of Africa’s ten biggest economies, status spending beats wealth-building 1.4–6× — verified, corrected and extended by AGF.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: The Price of “I Do” — What African Weddings Cost Relative to Income (2026)
item.description: A US wedding costs ~40% of a year’s average income. The average Nigerian wedding costs ~10 years’ worth. What Africans spend on weddings relative to income — fact-checked, bride price included, diaspora included.
item.dc:creator: Africa Global Forum

item.title: Africa Is Not Poor. Africa Is Under-Processed. — 2026
item.description: 51 of 54 countries export a raw commodity first — and 80–90% of the value is created after it leaves. The export map, the value-addition gap, and why the diaspora is the missing bridge.
